edges.mechanism: Lactose-derived GOS ingredients contain residual lactose (typically 20-40% DM) and free galactose (<=5% DM); classical galactosemia requires lifelong lactose restriction and galactosides may release absorbable galactose in the colon.
edges.evidence: International guideline, practice survey, GRAS specification, small dietary study; expert-level inference

edges.mechanism: IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to short-chain GOS (>=3 sugar units) in atopic, cow's-milk-tolerant patients; estimated allergy prevalence up to 3.5% in an atopic Singapore cohort.
edges.evidence: Case series with SPT/BAT and oral challenges; narrative review

edges.mechanism: Dietary GOS is a FODMAP; in blinded reintroduction it triggered symptoms in 35% of low-FODMAP responders and worsened pain and bloating. Low-dose beta-GOS (1.4-3.5 g/d) has, however, improved symptoms in RCTs.
edges.evidence: Blinded rechallenge RCTs, MA of prebiotics in IBS (null overall), 2026 fiber MA (beta-GOS subgroup benefit)

edges.mechanism: GOS is restricted during the elimination phase; low-dose B-GOS added to the diet improved response but did not prevent the fall in bifidobacteria.

RP-G28 GOS induces colonic adaptation (more lactose-fermenting bacteria) and improved symptoms; commercial GOS powders may themselves contain substantial lactose, and fermentation can cause transient symptoms.
edges.evidence: Phase 2 and 2b/3 RCTs, microbiome study, GRAS specification

edges.mechanism: Both are bifidogenic prebiotics; GOS/FOS and GOS/inulin mixtures are standard in infant and pregnancy trials.
edges.evidence: MA of fiber RCTs; RCTs of mixtures

edges.mechanism: Additive colonic fermentation: inulin-type fructans worsened flatulence in IBS MA, and fructans and GOS are the most prevalent FODMAP triggers.
edges.evidence: MA of prebiotics in IBS; blinded FODMAP rechallenge

edges.mechanism: Synbiotic pairing: GOS + B. lactis beat probiotic alone on FBG in T2DM; GOS + L. reuteri improved toddler bone/muscle outcomes and synergistically reduced colitis in mice.
edges.evidence: RCTs (n=120, n=182), preclinical study, narrative review

edges.mechanism: GOS co-ingestion increases fractional iron absorption ~30-60% (lower fecal pH, colonic absorption) and mitigates adverse microbiome effects of iron fortification in infants.
edges.evidence: Stable-isotope RCTs in women and infants; RCT in Kenyan infants; SR/MA (low certainty)

edges.mechanism: GOS enhancement of iron absorption is shown only for non-heme ferrous fumarate; no effect seen for ferrous sulfate in synbiotic formula and no data for heme iron.
edges.evidence: Indirect: stable-isotope studies; no heme-iron study

edges.mechanism: GOS taken during/after amoxicillin supported recovery of bifidobacteria and raised fecal butyrate; no effect on drug exposure known.
GOS alone did not change insulin sensitivity; a GOS+B. lactis synbiotic lowered FBG by 0.69 mmol/L vs placebo, so a small additive effect is possible with synbiotics.
GOS increases fractional/true calcium absorption, likely via lower-gut absorption mediated by bifidobacteria.
Enzyme reduces symptoms from alpha-linked GOS in legumes in GOS-sensitive IBS; not shown for beta-GOS supplements.
14.2 g/d GOS/FOS from mid-pregnancy had no safety signals; GDM reduced only in women with BMI >=25.
True physiological change: increased Bifidobacterium and decreased alpha-diversity at high dose; lower fecal pH in infants.
Co-administration with iron raises absorption and ferritin.
edges.evidence: SR/MA; RCT in children with HIV
